title: B.C. declares provincewide state of emergency as wildfires force thousands out of homes | CBC
text:
B.C. declares state of emergency due to wildfires burning across the province Wildfire state of emergency gives B.C. these powers Summerland, B.C., fire 'happened so fast,' says mayor Why these food boxes mean so much to wildfire evacuees Thousands of residents around Okanagan Lake forced to leave ahead of advancing flames B.C. wildfire evacuees process losing almost everything Hot, dry conditions continue to challenge wildfire fighters across much of B.C. Over 100 fires currently burning in BC. How Peachland, B.C., is preparing for wildfire evacuations Mayor Patrick Van Minsel explains the work underway to keep everyone safe as his community deals with approaching flames while housing evacuees from other areas. Peachland Mayor Patrick Van Minsel told CBC that no structures have been lost in his community due to the Bald Range fire. But he said his fire chief told him the blaze was unlike anything crews had ever dealt with. "He said they had never seen this before, the behaviour of this fire," Van Misnel said. The mayor estimated about 20 per cent of Peachland residents were placed under an evacuation order, and said police went door to door in the early morning hours alerting them to leave. "Most residents are calm — they're used to this. It's not our first rodeo," he said. Evacuees were sent north to an Emergency Support Services reception centre in West Kelowna, he said. Van Minsel said evacuation orders and alerts would remain in place at least overnight, and that officials would review the situation tomorrow. "I want people to know that our fire department is there, we're on it," he said, urging residents to be patient. "There are three [water] bombers here, they're now doing their job on the lake, and that we are very vigilant." The B.C. Wildfire Service says the Bald Range fire has now grown to more than 103 square kilometres. Meanwhile, the Penticton Indian Band has issued an evacuation order for half a dozen properties, along with an alert for a similar number of addresses. The Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen also expanded an evacuation alert for a number of properties in an area south of Summerland and west of Penticton. People in the Greater West Bench and Kickininee Park areas, the Brent Lake and Shingle Creek areas and Farleigh Lake Road area have been told to be ready to leave on a moment's notice. The Bald Range fire has swept through some of the Okanagan's prime agricultural land during the peak of the region's summer harvest. Among the evacuees are about 40 migrant workers who say they were taken by bus from the cherry farm where they were working and brought to West Kelowna, where temporary accommodation has been set up at the Royal LePage arena. One worker told me it was a frightening experience as the fire approached, saying the stress of the situation made it difficult to sleep last night in the cots provided for evacuees. Volunteers with the Okanagan Central Salvation Army are providing hot meals today as evacuees wait to learn if there is other accommodation available. Why these food boxes mean so much to wildfire evacuees Volunteers in West Kelowna have been feeding wildfire evacuees with full meals and easy-to-grab boxes filled with instant foods. Trevor Moss, CEO of the Central Okanagan Food Bank, explains the feedback he has received on why the boxes are so important to those who need them. Volunteers with the Central Okanagan Food Bank and the Okanagan Central Salvation Army are providing hot meals and food packages to Summerland and Peachland evacuees who are taking shelter at a hockey arena in West Kelowna. Many evacuees spent the night here on cots and are now waiting to register with Emergency Support Services. Trevor Moss, CEO of the Central Okanagan Food Bank, says volunteers have prepared more than 300 food boxes for evacuees. These boxes include local fruits, yogurt packages, snacks and instant meals that can be made in a hotel room. "What we have learned from the fires from 2023 is that these little things matter. It touches lives and we couldn't do this with the generous help of the community," Moss said. RCMP in British Columbia say they are investigating a possible fatality in the massive fire near Summerland. Southeast District RCMP said in a statement that a resident of Meadow Valley, west of Summerland, has reported the possible death. They say police and the B.C. Coroners Service are working on confirmation, but there are hazardous conditions in the area. RCMP said officers are "working closely with the impacted family." In Peachland, some residents — including some evacuees — have been on the lakeshore watching B.C. Wildfire Service planes load up with water from Okanagan Lake to dump on the fire. People are also yelling at boaters to get off the lake. On more than one occasion a plane was unable to load up because of boats on the water. I even heard a plane sound its alarm siren to indicate that people need to leave. Boaters near Peachland: we see you! Please stay clear of wildfire suppression aircraft. 🚁❌🛥️

Please stay off the lake near active firefighting operations and give BC Wildfire Service the space they need to protect our communities. pic.twitter.com/bmtGgZlsmD I'm a reporter for CBC based in Kelowna. I spent yesterday evening and today speaking with evacuees who fled their homes in Summerland and Peachland as the Bald Range fire burned closer to those communities. Many people spent last night sleeping on cots at Royal LePage Arena in West Kelowna, where evacuees are receiving emergency support and shelter. Tom Bennie left his Summerland home around 7:30 p.m. last night when he saw flames crest a hill close to the downtown area. He says he's concerned the fire may have reached the apartment building where he lives and the home-based business equipment he had to leave behind. Bennie and his partner are among the many people waiting to speak with Emergency Support Services to register and learn about accommodation options. Interior Health says families can call 1-833-971-5045 to get updates on loved ones who were evacuated from care homes. Forty-eight residents were evacuated from the Dr. Andrew Pavillion long-term care home in Summerland, the regional health authority said. Another 190 were evacuated from Summerland Seniors Village. "Wherever possible, IH has contacted families directly with updates to share their loved ones' temporary location. The call centre is an additional tool for families who could not be reached directly," it said. The call centre will operate from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. PT today and tomorrow, and from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. PT from Monday to Friday. Jennifer Pascoa says when she saw flames getting closer in Summerland last night, she started to pack up and make plans to leave. "It happened so quickly. We came home from the beach, we saw the plume of smoke, and then within an hour, the sky was covered in dark, black clouds," Pascoa told CBC News from Penticton, where she and her daughter have sought shelter at the city's convention centre. While the situation was scary, Pascoa said the evacuation was "eerily calm" because they were well prepared and knew where to go. Her daughter Emery said she was nervous, though. "I went through about six different emotions during that time, and I just wanted to make sure all the younger kids were OK and calm and not too scared," Emery said. Pascoa said the family has received an outpouring of support in Penticton. "Every 15 minutes, it seems, someone's coming up and asking us if they can get us anything." At the Elks Hall in Penticton, volunteers are busy making hundreds of sandwiches for evacuees. This morning, they brought over 400 breakfasts to the evacuation centre. Canteen manager Deborah Sayese said they're happy to help where they can. "The most we can do is make sure people have something to eat and make sure people aren't clamouring around for food," Sayese said. Her team is making around 300 sandwiches for evacuees today — and another 300 for tomorrow. Audience Relations, CBC P.O.
